Up to six months after the second dose, 412 of 1182 participants in the vaccine group and 201 of 1146 participants in the comparator group experienced any grade adverse events. Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably increase the number of participants with any grade adverse events up to six months after the second dose compared to placebo or no vaccine (RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.30; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence; Analysis 4.3 ). We downgraded the certainty of the evidence by one level for serious indirectness due to the mixed population. Serious adverse events One RCT reported data on any grade adverse events, including 2328 participants with solid tumours and haematological malignancies who had a past or ongoing malignancy ( Thomas 2022 ). Participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta, and gamma. Up to six months after the second dose, 28 of 1182 participants in the vaccine group and 19 of 1146 participants in the comparator group experienced any grade adverse events. Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 may make little or no difference in the number of participants with serious adverse events up to six months after the second dose compared to placebo or no vaccine (RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.54; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; low‐certainty evidence; Analysis 4.4 ). We downgraded the certainty of the evidence by one level for serious indirectness due to the mixed population and by one level due to a wide confidence interval. Localised events at the injection site We did not identify any RCT or controlled NRSI reporting this outcome. Systemic events We did not identify any RCT or controlled NRSI reporting this outcome. Vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine We identified no RCTs or controlled NRSIs comparing vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria versus placebo or no vaccine. Discussion Summary of main results This review aimed to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours. Altogether, we identified 10 studies for inclusion in this review. Most studies included adults with malignant solid tumours of different types. Of these, three RCTs (3054 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster, five studies (one RCT and four controlled NRSIs; 76,372 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza, and one RCT (2256 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent COVID‐19. The RCTs assessing herpes zoster and COVID‐19 vaccines were funded by the manufacturers of the vaccines. We assessed the RCTs as being at low or moderate risk of bias, while we judged most of the controlled NRSIs to be at critical risk of bias, primarily due to concerns about confounding. Further, we identified two ongoing studies: one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine and one controlled NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines. We also identified one completed but not yet published study, and 11 studies await classification due to unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest, results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination. We did not identify RCTs or controlled NRSIs on vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. In the following, only the results from RCTs are presented. Results from controlled NRSIs are detailed in the Effects of interventions section of the main text. Effects of interventions Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 1 . Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster decrease the incidence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster probably make little or no difference in all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after the final dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster make little or no difference in adverse events (any grade) up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence) and probably make little or no difference in serious adverse events up to 30 days (moderate certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster increase the number of participants with localised events at the injection site up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster may have little or no difference in the number of participants with systemic events up to 30 days after the final dose (low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 2 . We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on all‐cause mortality up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza in adverse events (any grade) up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on serious adverse events up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 3 . Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in participants without previous COVID‐19 infection up to six months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably increase the number of participants with adverse events (any grade) up to 6 months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 may make little or no difference in the number of participants with serious adverse events up to 6 months after the second dose (low‐certainty evidence). Overall completeness and applicability of evidence The evidence summarised in this systematic review applies to vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster, influenza, and COVID‐19 in adults with solid tumours. The findings are particularly relevant for healthcare providers involved in the care of these people, as they can guide vaccination strategies aimed at reducing infection risk. Understanding vaccine efficacy and safety is crucial for adults with solid tumours when making informed health decisions. The review indicates that certain vaccines, specifically those for herpes zoster and COVID‐19, demonstrate high‐ or moderate‐certainty evidence for reducing infection incidence. However, these vaccines may be associated with localised events at the injection site or any‐grade adverse events. It is important to note that the applicability of these findings may vary based on specific types of malignancy and their stages. Additionally, cancer therapies can significantly impact immune function and vaccine efficacy. However, due to insufficient data, we could not determine whether there are differences in outcomes between various malignancies or cancer therapies. The RCTs on herpes zoster included adults with diverse solid tumour types, such as breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and lung cancer ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ), all receiving chemotherapy. This diversity allows for some comparison regarding how chemotherapy impacts vaccine efficacy across different cancers. Additionally, there are variations in vaccine types used in these studies. In Mullane 2013 , participants received a heat‐treated zoster vaccine, while Mullane 2019 administered an inactivated varicella‐zoster virus vaccine. In contrast, Vink 2019 employed an adjuvant recombinant zoster vaccine. A distinction in vaccine types may be important because different formulations can elicit varying immune responses, which may impact their effectiveness. In contrast to the herpes zoster vaccines, the RCT on influenza vaccines focused on adults with neck and oesophageal cancers undergoing surgery ( Goldmann 2015 ). This may limit the generalisability of the findings to other cancer types or treatment modalities, since participants were vaccinated prior to surgery. While there is very low certainty in the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of influenza vaccination for this particular subset of patients, it may not directly apply to those receiving immunotherapy or other surgical interventions. To supplement our findings from Goldmann 2015 , which was published as correspondence, we incorporated data from controlled NRSIs. For instance, INVIDIa‐2 and Amdisen 2024 reported on the incidence of influenza across a wider range of cancers, including participants undergoing immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy or chemotherapy. However, the studies primarily focused on severe disease and may not capture milder cases or asymptomatic infections, which are also important for assessing vaccine efficacy. In contrast, the data from controlled NRSI suggests that there is an effect on all‐cause mortality (moderate‐certainty) ( Gögenur 2021 ). This difference may arise from the different populations and the timing of the vaccination analysed in the included studies. Gögenur 2021 focuses on post‐surgery vaccination across multiple cancer types scheduled for surgery. The timing of the vaccination was within 30 days post‐surgery. The study measured all‐cause mortality as an outcome 180 days to three years post‐surgery. Nevertheless, this long‐term follow‐up provides insights into the potential impact of post‐surgery influenza vaccination on survival outcomes, thereby enhancing the completeness of results. However, while this study increases applicability by addressing diverse patient populations, it is essential to consider that factors influencing mortality may be multifactorial and not solely attributable to vaccination status. With respect to any‐grade adverse events, there remains uncertainty regarding the effects of influenza vaccines as indicated by both RCT ( Goldmann 2015 ) and controlled NRSI ( Wijn 2018 ) data. Wijn 2018 focused on adults with lung cancer receiving nivolumab. The study provides insights into the interactions between seasonal influenza vaccination and immunotherapy, but their targeted nature may restrict generalisability to other cancer treatments or patient populations not undergoing similar therapies. Influenza viruses are constantly evolving, and new strains can emerge. Influenza vaccines are adjusted annually to ensure better efficacy against the currently circulating strains ( WHO 2024 ). Therefore, it is important to interpret our findings on influenza vaccines with caution, as the included studies cover various influenza seasons. For example, the study by INVIDIa‐2 focuses on the 2019/2020 influenza season, while Wijn 2018 investigates the 2015/2016 and 2016/2017 seasons and Amdisen 2024 covers the seasons 2007/2008 to 2017/2018. Gögenur 2021 recruited participants between 2010 and 2015, and Goldmann 2015 covers the period from 2005 to 2008. This variability means that studies conducted across different seasons may yield results that are not directly comparable or applicable to current strains circulating within specific populations. In terms of COVID‐19 vaccines, Thomas 2022 focused on adults with various solid tumours, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, but did not provide clear information about specific cancer treatments received by the participants. We used data from a mixed population of solid tumours and haematological malignancies for adverse events and serious adverse events analyses since we expect similar events across both groups ( Copeland 2024 ; Javadinia 2022 ). Based on the RCT data, COVID‐19 vaccines probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 (moderate‐certainty). As the data only originates from a post‐hoc subgroup analysis, we supplemented our findings with data from controlled NRSIs. In contrast, controlled NRSI data presents uncertainty regarding their effects. The controlled NRSI by Zhao 2024 , specifically examined adults with hepatocellular carcinoma, a group facing unique immunological challenges due to liver dysfunction and underlying viral infections (e.g. hepatitis), which could influence vaccine efficacy differently than in other solid tumours ( Sachdeva 2015 ). Moreover, differences in vaccination regimens complicate comparisons. Thomas 2022 used the BNT162b2 vaccine, while Zhao 2024 , included multiple vaccines such as CoronaVac, BBIBP‐CorV, Zifivax, Convidecia, and BNT162b2. Notably, in Zhao 2024 , a small proportion of participants (6.5%) were not fully vaccinated. Such an incomplete vaccination status could lead to underestimating the potential protective effect of vaccination against infection. Furthermore, Thomas 2022 recruited participants between July 2020 to January 2021. Based on the recruitment period, we assume that participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta and gamma. In contrast, Zhao 2024 recruited participants between January 2022 and October 2022 where omicron was prevalent. The evidence is only applicable to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants prevalent at the time of the studies. It is also crucial for consumers and caregivers to be aware of the limitations regarding other vaccines due to insufficient data. Although there is a lack of evidence or only low to very low‐certainty evidence for many of the vaccines we were interested in for this particular group of adults with solid tumours, studies involving immunocompetent adults generally demonstrate that vaccines are well tolerated and effective in preventing severe outcomes and providing protection ( Demicheli 2018 ; Graña 2022 ; Plosker 2015 ). Due to the small number of included studies and lack of subgroup data in the primary studies, we were unable to adequately investigate the influence of effect modifiers, such as type of malignancy or treatment, through subgroup analyses. While most studies measure immunogenicity parameters such as antibody levels, seroconversion, or T‐cell responses, there are no correlates of protection defined. These surrogate endpoints are not considered as patient‐relevant outcomes. In this review, we focused only on patient‐relevant outcomes that we determined in a workshop conducted with people with cancer and their representatives. The involvement of adults with cancer and their representatives was essential to obtain a better understanding of patient‐important outcomes, to ensure a patient‐relevant focus for this systematic review, and to ensure that our findings remain relevant to consumers navigating complex healthcare decisions. Notably, none of the included studies measured quality of life. The studies included in our review were predominantly conducted in high‐income countries, which may not fully represent the challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). According to Kamboj 2024 , the availability, accessibility, and utilisation of vaccines amongst adults with cancer in LMICs present significant hurdles. Limited resources and infrastructure, along with logistical barriers, often hinder vaccine distribution in these regions. Additionally, the high cost of vaccines can render them financially unattainable for many individuals. Consequently, the lack of access to vaccines leaves individuals with cancer in LMICs vulnerable to serious infections, which can adversely impact their health outcomes. Our review identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one controlled NRSI ( NCT05774171 ) evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines, which may provide further insights into vaccine efficacy once they are completed. One RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine has been completed, but no results have been published yet ( NCT02998736 ). We further categorised 12 studies with unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest or results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination as 'awaiting classification' ( Bettinger 2022 ; EPIVAC ; Hayashi 2023 ; Kazemain 2023 ; Khaddour 2022 ; Klastersky 1986 ; Lau 2022 ; Leuva 2022 ; NCT01698177 ; NL‐OMON32477 ; Serrano 2022 ; Vinograd 2013 ). EPIVAC , a comprehensive population‐based cohort study, assessed the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines and provided data categorised for individuals with compromised immune systems. These encompass solid tumours, haematological malignancies, chronic severe nephropathy, asplenia, immunodeficiency (including HIV), and long‐term corticosteroid therapy or other immunosuppressive drugs. Since the data for these conditions were not analysed separately, we were unable to include the study. We will consider including these studies in an update of this review once results or sufficient information is available. Furthermore, we excluded numerous controlled NRSIs in which healthy individuals were used as a control group (e.g. Gomez 2021 ; Silveira 2019 ). Quality of the evidence Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from three RCTs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as high to low (see Table 1 ). We have high certainty in the evidence for the outcomes of incidence of herpes zoster, adverse events of any grade, and localised events at the injection site, and moderate certainty for the outcomes of all‐cause mortality and serious adverse events. Our main concern was imprecision due to wide confidence intervals. We have low certainty in the identified evidence for systemic events. We downgraded the certainty of the evidence for imprecision due to a wide confidence interval and inconsistency due to substantial statistical heterogeneity. Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT and four controlled NRSIs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low (see Table 2 ). For the RCT, we rated the certainty of the evidence as very low. Our main concerns were the risk of bias due to missing information on allocation concealment, missing data, selection of the reported results, and imprecision due to very wide confidence intervals, low number of participants, and low number of events (all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, and serious adverse events). For controlled NRSIs, we rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low. We downgraded the evidence for risk of bias due to confounding (incidence of influenza, all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade) and imprecision due to wide confidence intervals (incidence of influenza, adverse events of any grade). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to low (see Table 3 ). Our main concerns were imprecision due to a low number of events or wide confidence intervals (incidence of COVID‐19, serious adverse events), or indirectness due to a mixed population including participants with solid tumours and haematological malignancies (any‐grade adverse events and serious adverse events). Potential biases in the review process We followed the guidelines of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions to minimise several potential biases in the review process ( Higgins 2024a ). An experienced information specialist (IM) developed the peer‐reviewed search strategy. The sensitive search included relevant electronic databases, as well as clinical trial registries, to ensure comprehensive coverage of available literature. To uphold the integrity and reliability of our review process, we conducted a comprehensive search for errata and retractions related to the studies included in our analysis. This step was essential for identifying potential biases arising from flawed or retracted research that could impact our conclusions. To supplement the lack of RCTs, we performed searches for controlled NRSIs when no RCTs were available for vaccines targeting specific infectious diseases. This also included vaccines to prevent influenza and COVID‐19, as the identified RCTs were published as correspondence ( Goldmann 2015 ) or reported data on solid tumour participants in a post hoc subgroup analysis ( Thomas 2022 ). While correspondence and post hoc analyses might provide valuable insights, they are generally considered less informative compared to primary research articles. Due to the limitations of these publication types, we decided to search for controlled NRSI as well. Given the differences in study design and potential biases associated with controlled NRSIs, we did not pool data from RCTs and controlled NRSIs. In addition, we made a conscious decision to categorise eligible studies that did not report any relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification' rather than including or excluding them without having explored other ways to establish if our outcomes had been measured. This change reflects our commitment to ensuring that only studies with pertinent outcome data contribute to our findings. We included only studies with a minimum sample size of 20 participants per arm. This criterion was established to enhance the reliability and generalisability of our findings by ensuring that included studies had sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful effects. However, this inclusion criterion may also limit the number of available studies, potentially introducing bias if smaller but relevant studies are excluded from consideration (e.g. Chu 2013 ; Kumar 2012 ). In classifying interventions and outcomes, we based our decisions on the data available from the studies. We categorised the studies according to their design (RCTs versus controlled NRSIs) and focused on outcomes that were deemed important by adults with cancer and their representatives. Further, we distinguished between 'localised events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' as separate outcomes. Nonetheless, it is important to note that some studies reported symptoms such as headache or fever as single outcomes, which limited our ability to analyse these effects together ( Thomas 2022 ; Zhao 2024 ). In our analysis, we aimed to capture long‐term outcomes by using the longest available follow‐up data. However, this approach may present limitations, particularly due to variability in follow‐up durations across studies. Such differences may lead to inconsistencies in outcome reporting, introduce potential biases in assessing long‐term effects, and challenges in comparing results between studies with varying timeframes. In cases of missing data, if we needed more information, we contacted the study authors for additional data or relevant details. We received answers from the contact authors of three studies ( Amdisen 2024 ; Leuva 2022 ; Mullane 2013 ). However, we could not use the data from Leuva 2022 due to unclear follow‐up time after a full vaccination. The data from Amdisen 2024 were measured as incidence rates per 10,000 person‐years for the outcomes of incidence of influenza and all‐cause mortality. Due to the incompatible format of these outcomes, we only provide a narrative description, without assessing the risk of bias or certainty of the evidence. Given the small number of studies included in each comparison, the informative value of statistical methods for analysing publication bias, such as funnel plots, was limited. Moreover, due to the small number of included studies, we were unable to conduct any subgroup analyses that might have provided further insights into specific populations or intervention effects. Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews Notably, the ASCO guidelines addressed a research question similar to ours by systematically reviewing studies published between 2013 and 2023 ( Kamboj 2024 ). They focused on adults with solid tumours or haematological malignancies, including long‐term survivors and those who received haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, evaluating routine vaccines listed on the CDC immunisation schedules as well as travel vaccines. Their comparisons included placebo, different vaccines, or varying vaccination strategies. The outcomes assessed encompassed risk of infection, disease severity, mortality, immune responses, and vaccine safety ( Kamboj 2024 ). In terms of herpes zoster vaccines, Kamboj 2024 identified a study concerning solid tumours reporting adverse events ( Vink 2019 ), but did not include Mullane 2013 and Mullane 2019 as the guidelines focused on recombinant zoster vaccines (RZV). RZV, commonly known by its brand name Shingrix, is a recombinant form of glycoprotein E from the varicella‐zoster virus, which is a key protein involved in the virus's ability to infect cells ( Vink 2019 ). Our findings on herpes zoster vaccines align with those of a network meta‐analysis conducted by Xia 2022 , which reported that RZV demonstrated superior efficacy compared to placebo in immunocompromised individuals, achieving 60% efficacy (95% CI 49% to 69%). Adverse events associated with RZV were primarily related to injection site reactions and systemic effects, with no increased risk of serious adverse events or death. Kamboj 2024 indicated that "grade three solicited general adverse events" (i.e. moderate‐to‐severe adverse events actively monitored during the study), were reported by adults with cancer in both the vaccine and placebo arms but were more prevalent in the vaccine arms. This finding is consistent with our observations regarding the safety profile of herpes zoster vaccines. However, it is important to highlight that the analyses by Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 exclusively included studies assessing RZV, while our review encompassed studies assessing heat‐treated zoster vaccines ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ). Additionally, Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 included studies across various immunocompromised conditions such as haematological malignancies, renal transplantation, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and HIV, alongside one study involving individuals with solid tumours ( Vink 2019 ), which was also part of our review. A previous Cochrane review on influenza vaccination conducted by Bitterman 2018 demonstrated that influenza vaccination is associated with reduced mortality and lower rates of infection‐related outcomes compared to non‐vaccination. This review encompassed a diverse population, including adults with solid tumours, haematological malignancies, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The inclusion of such a broad range of immunocompromised groups suggests that influenza vaccination may confer significant benefits across these populations. However, more recent systematic reviews have provided additional insights into the effects of influenza vaccination specifically in adults with cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. For instance, a systematic review by Tsiakos 2022 indicated that influenza vaccination appeared to have no effect on the mortality of adults with cancer receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Furthermore, it presented an acceptable safety profile, as it was not associated with an increased incidence of immune‐related adverse events, whether any grade or serious. In line with this, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 reported that vaccinated adults with cancer exhibited slightly lower rates of immune‐related adverse events compared to unvaccinated adults with cancer (32% versus 41%), reinforcing the notion that vaccination does not exacerbate safety concerns. Despite these findings, both reviews highlight the limitations in available data regarding other efficacy and safety outcomes. Tsiakos 2022 noted that limited data exist concerning progression‐free survival, humoral immunity response, cell‐mediated immunity response, and the incidence of influenza. Similarly, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 provided specific metrics indicating seroprotection rates for different influenza types (78% to 79% for type A and 75% for type B) but did not address these additional outcomes. However, most of the data are derived from observational retrospective studies with small sample sizes and unadjusted analyses ( Lopez‐Olivo 2022 ; Tsiakos 2022 ). The Cochrane review by Graña 2022 concluded that most COVID‐19 vaccines reduce or likely reduce the occurrence of confirmed symptomatic COVID‐19 when compared to placebo. For some vaccines, there is high‐certainty evidence supporting their effectiveness in reducing severe or critical disease. Our findings align with this conclusion, as we also observed a reduction in the incidence of COVID‐19 amongst vaccinated participants without previous infection (moderate‐certainty evidence). Kamboj 2024 further reported numerous studies examining immunologic parameters related to COVID‐19 vaccination amongst adults with cancer. They identified five controlled NRSIs demonstrating reduced rates of hospitalisation and mortality or decreased COVID‐19 sequelae in vaccinated versus unvaccinated adults with cancer. However, these studies did not exclusively focus on adults with solid tumours but also included adults with haematological malignancies ( Kamboj 2024 ). This broader inclusion may account for some variability in outcomes, but it underscores the importance of vaccination across different cancer types. In terms of vaccine safety, our observations regarding adverse events are consistent with those reported by Javadinia 2022 , who noted that COVID‐19 vaccination in adults with cancer is generally well‐tolerated regardless of cancer type. Both systemic and local adverse events, including fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, asthenia, vomiting, headaches, muscle and joint pain, chills, transient lymphadenopathy, and injection site reactions, were reported across various studies. While Javadinia 2022 highlighted that most vaccine‐related side effects were grade two at most, they also pointed out the challenges posed by differing assessment methods across studies, which complicate meta‐analysis efforts, such as the lack of reporting on the exact prevalence of PCR‐confirmed COVID‐19 infections and their outcomes. Additionally, many studies included in their review lacked a control group or used healthy controls, complicating the analysis still further ( Javadinia 2022 ). Our review reveals notable gaps in the literature concerning other vaccines. Kamboj 2024 reported an absence of eligible studies for hepatitis B, tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccines. This lack of data aligns with our findings regarding the limited research available on certain vaccinations for adults with solid tumours. Furthermore, Kamboj 2024 identified only one RCT that examined the timing of pneumococcal vaccination. Authors' conclusions Implications for practice In adults with solid tumours, herpes zoster vaccines reduce the incidence of herpes zoster (high‐certainty evidence), although localised events at the injection site occur more frequently than with placebo or no vaccine (high‐certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether influenza vaccines affect all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, or serious adverse events (very‐low certainty evidence); the incidence of influenza was not measured in the studies. Vaccines for preventing COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in adults without prior infection (moderate‐certainty evidence), but they probably increase adverse events of any grade (moderate‐certainty evidence). We found no randomised controlled trials or controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions that investigated the use of vaccines compared to placebo or no vaccine for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, in adults with solid tumours. Implications for research We have identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines ( NCT05774171 ). Additional research, preferably RCTs, is necessary to assess a wider range of available vaccines against infectious diseases such as pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, for which we did not identify any RCTs or prospective NRSIs. This lack of research limits our understanding of how these vaccines perform in adults with solid tumours. While we advocate conducting RCTs to obtain robust evidence, if such studies are not possible for ethical reasons, retrospective (matched) analyses of individuals with cancer who have or have not received the respective vaccination could provide some insights. Future studies should include individuals of various age groups and those with different types of solid tumours undergoing diverse treatments (such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy). This diversity is crucial, because different age groups may respond differently to vaccines due to variations in immune system function, and individuals with solid tumours may be undergoing treatments that affect their immune response. When investigating multiple malignancies, it is important to report results as subgroups. This approach allows researchers to identify specific populations that benefit most from vaccination and understand under which cancer therapies the vaccines may be less effective in preventing infection. Additionally, it needs to be investigated whether passive immunisation with monoclonal antibodies may offer more protection than vaccines for immunocompromised or immunosuppressed individuals. Research should not just focus on the usual immunological laboratory parameters, especially in populations where established correlates of protection are still lacking. The outcomes measured should be patient‐centred and important, such as the incidence of infection (tracking how often vaccinated individuals contract the targeted infectious disease), quality of life (assessing how vaccination impacts patients' overall well‐being and daily functioning), all‐cause mortality (evaluating whether vaccination correlates with mortality rates amongst individuals with solid tumours), and adverse events (monitoring any negative side effects resulting from vaccination). Additionally, studies should take into account periods when the risk of infection is heightened. For instance, during flu season (typically October to March), individuals with compromised immune systems may face increased risks. Future research should investigate potential effect modifiers that could influence the effectiveness of vaccines for preventing infectious diseases. These might include patient demographics (age, sex, comorbidities) and treatment modalities (type and timing of cancer therapies). Importantly, future research must also address the unique challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), where barriers such as limited healthcare infrastructure, vaccine availability, and socioeconomic factors can significantly impact vaccination efforts. By understanding how these characteristics impact vaccine efficacy in LMIC contexts, alongside other factors influencing outcomes in high‐income settings, healthcare providers can tailor vaccination strategies to individual patient needs more effectively. In summary, addressing these gaps through rigorous research will enhance our understanding of vaccine effects across diverse patient populations. By prioritising patient‐centred outcomes and considering various factors influencing vaccine efficacy, including those specific to LMICs, we can optimise vaccination strategies to improve health outcomes for individuals at risk for infectious diseases. between protocol and review Differences between the published protocol ( Bora 2023 ) and this full review are as follows. Title We made minor edits to the title in order to use UK spelling ('tumours') and Cochrane style, i.e. 'for preventing' rather than 'for the prevention of'. Objectives We changed the wording from "To assess the benefits and harms of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours" to "To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours." Type of interventions We changed the wording to "We included vaccines for the prevention of the following infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours" and listed the diseases of the vaccines they protect against instead of the pathogens to specify the diseases targeted by these vaccines. Types of outcome measures Instead of including studies regardless of the reported outcome data, we decided to categorise eligible studies that did not report any of the relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification'. We previously listed 'local events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' under the outcome 'adverse events of special interest'. As these were intended to represent two separate outcomes, we no longer summarise them under one bullet point in the review but list them separately. Selection of studies We used the Rayyan software ( Ouzzani 2016 ) instead of Covidence to screen the references. We listed excluded studies that initially appeared to meet the inclusion criteria, but that we later excluded, in the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table, with the reasons for their exclusion, instead of listing all excluded studies. Search methods Although at least one RCT was identified for vaccines against influenza and COVID‐19, we searched for NRSIs, as the one RCT on influenza vaccines was published as correspondence only, and the one RCT on COVID‐19 reported on participants with solid tumours in a post hoc subgroup analysis. To ensure the integrity and reliability of the studies included in this review, we searched for errata or retractions related to the included studies that may have been published on MEDLINE, Embase, or Retraction Watch. We did not contact experts in the field to retrieve information on unpublished studies. If required, we contacted the authors for supplementary information. Assessment of reporting bias As we did not pool the data in the meta‐analysis and included fewer than 10 studies per comparison, we did not generate funnel plots to assess reporting bias. Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity We removed the planned subgroup analysis based on duration of follow‐up (e.g. shorter versus longer follow‐up) because we grouped the measurement time points of eligible outcomes into short‐term (up to 12 weeks after full vaccination), medium‐term (from 12 weeks to 6 months after full vaccination) and long‐term (more than 6 months after full vaccination) observations, if sufficient data was available (see Types of outcome measures ). Due to the limited number of studies that provided relevant data for our critical outcome, we did not perform meta‐analysis and thus conducted no subgroup analysis. If heterogeneity was above 75%, we planned to explore this with subgroup and sensitivity analysis. Despite considerable heterogeneity in Analysis 1.5 , we decided to keep the pooled effect estimate, as the effects of the individual studies were clearly on one side. We were unable to conduct the planned sensitivity analyses because the risk of bias for these RCTs was classified as either 'low' or 'some concerns'. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We created the summary of findings tables manually and did not use GRADEpro GDT . We added a section on consumer involvement during protocol development. The order of the comparisons and summary of findings tables was prioritised by clinical experts, based on relevance to decision‐makers. If evidence from both RCTs and NRSIs was available for a single outcome, only the RCT data were presented in the summary of findings tables. documents.title: Effectiveness of tofacitinib in patients with ulcerative colitis: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of real-world studies.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the real-world effectiveness of tofacitinib for treating moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC).
DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane CENTRAL databases were searched from inception up to 18 July 2023. Reference lists of included studies were manually searched to identify potentially relevant studies not found in the databases.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Eligible studies included real-world observational studies, reported in English, on patients with moderate-to-severe UC treated with tofacitinib, defined by the Partial Mayo Score. Excluded were clinical trials, reviews, letters, conference abstracts, case reports and studies involving patients with mixed Crohn's disease.
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Two independent reviewers extracted data and recorded it in Excel. Quality assessment was performed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale. Meta-analysis was performed using random-effects models due to high heterogeneity across studies.
RESULTS: 19 studies containing a total of 2612 patients were included. Meta-analysis revealed that clinical response rates were 58% at week 8, 61% at weeks 12-16, 51% at weeks 24-26 and 51% at week 52. Clinical remission rates were 39% at week 8, 43% at weeks 12-16, 40% at weeks 24-26 and 43% at week 52. Corticosteroid-free clinical remission rates were 33% at week 8, 37% at weeks 12-16, 32% at weeks 24-26 and 40% at week 52.
CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis of real-world studies indicates that treatment of UC with tofacitinib is associated with favourable clinical response and remission rates in the induction and maintenance phases.
documents.conclusions: This meta-analysis of real-world studies indicates that treatment of UC with tofacitinib is associated with favourable clinical response and remission rates in the induction and maintenance phases.

Abstract Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the real-world effectiveness of tofacitinib for treating moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC). Design Systematic review and meta-analysis. Data sources PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane CENTRAL databases were searched from inception up to 18 July 2023. Reference lists of included studies were manually searched to identify potentially relevant studies not found in the databases. Eligibility criteria Eligible studies included real-world observational studies, reported in English, on patients with moderate-to-severe UC treated with tofacitinib, defined by the Partial Mayo Score. Excluded were clinical trials, reviews, letters, conference abstracts, case reports and studies involving patients with mixed Crohn’s disease. Data extraction and synthesis Two independent reviewers extracted data and recorded it in Excel. Quality assessment was performed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale. Meta-analysis was performed using random-effects models due to high heterogeneity across studies. Results 19 studies containing a total of 2612 patients were included. Meta-analysis revealed that clinical response rates were 58% at week 8, 61% at weeks 12–16, 51% at weeks 24–26 and 51% at week 52. Clinical remission rates were 39% at week 8, 43% at weeks 12–16, 40% at weeks 24–26 and 43% at week 52. Corticosteroid-free clinical remission rates were 33% at week 8, 37% at weeks 12–16, 32% at weeks 24–26 and 40% at week 52. Conclusion This meta-analysis of real-world studies indicates that treatment of UC with tofacitinib is associated with favourable clinical response and remission rates in the induction and maintenance phases. Keywords: CLINICAL TRIALS, COLORECTAL DISEASES, DRUG METABOLISM, ULCERATIVE COLITIS, META-ANALYSIS status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2024 Jan 9; Accepted 2024 Oct 24; Collection date 2024. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Clinical trials have established the efficacy of tofacitinib in treating ulcerative colitis (UC). However, the relevance of these findings to real-world scenarios remains uncertain. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS The systematic review and meta-analysis offers insights into the efficacy of tofacitinib in treating UC based on the latest real-world data. Notably, it extends the analysis of tofacitinib’s effects to 52 weeks post-treatment initiation. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings provide clinicians and policy-makers with real-world evidence to guide treatment decisions and shape guidelines for UC. Introduction Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a recurring, chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterised by mucosal inflammation that begins in the distal regions of the colon and can extend upward, ultimately affecting the entire colon. 1 In 2023, it was estimated that UC affected approximately 5 million individuals globally, with a rising global incidence. 2 While UC can manifest at any age, it most commonly occurs between the ages of 20 and 40, with roughly equal frequency in men and women. 3 Traditional treatments for UC include mesalamine, glucocorticoids, immunomodulators and biologics offer relief to some patients. 4 However, despite progress in treatment methods, clinical remission is only achieved in a relatively small number of patients. 5 Tofacitinib has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of UC. Controlled clinical trials have shown that oral tofacitinib is effective for treating UC in adults and is associated with high clinical response and clinical remission rates. 6–10 Tofacitinib is a reversible, competitive inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK), specifically targeting JAK1 and JAK3. Inhibition prevents the phosphorylation of JAK proteins, thereby blocking the activation of the STAT pathway and downstream signalling of cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-15 and IL-21, as well as the production of proinflammatory proteins associated with mucosal inflammation. 11 Although clinical trials have shown that tofacitinib is effective for treating UC and has an acceptable safety profile, findings from controlled trials are not always the same as when the drug is used in an uncontrolled clinical practice. Real-world studies can assess tofacitinib’s performance in diverse patient populations, taking into consideration factors such as demographics, comorbidities, concurrent medications and treatment adherence. 12 Previous meta-analyses and systematic reviews, which have included data from real-world studies, have suggested that tofacitinib is a safe and effective treatment for UC. However, it is worth noting that the most recent studies included in these reviews only extended up to 2021. Additionally, few studies have examined the effectiveness of tofacitinib at 1 year after beginning treatment. 13 14 Thus, our purpose was to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effectiveness of tofacitinib for treating UC using only data from real-world studies. In addition, the analysis includes studies that provide outcome data at 1 year or more after beginning treatment. 15 Methods Search strategy The current systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines 15 ( online supplemental file, PRISMA checklist ). We conducted a comprehensive literature search of public databases including PubMed and EMBASE, for studies published from inception up to 18 July 2023. The specific keywords “tofacitinib”, “ulcerative colitis” and “real-world” were combined with Boolean operators and Medical Subject-Headings (MeSH) terms where appropriate were used in the searches to identify eligible studies. The exact search string used for PubMed and EMBASE was Supplementary data bmjgast-11-1-s003.pdf ( tofacitinib OR XELJANZ) AND (“ulcerative colitis”) AND (real-world OR observational ). In addition, we conducted a handsearch of the reference lists in the included studies to identify any potentially relevant studies not identified in the database searches. Two reviewers independently screened the citations for eligibility to ensure accuracy and reliability in the selection process. Selection criteria This review was conducted following the PICOS criteria, which is based on participants (P), interventions (I), comparisons (C), outcomes (O) and study design (S). Eligible studies were those including patients with moderate-to-severe, active UC (P) who were treated with tofacitinib (I). The severity of UC is characterised by the Partial Mayo Score (PMS), which includes stool frequency, rectal bleeding and physician’s global assessment. Moderate-to-severe UC is typically defined by a PMS of 5–9. The comparator group could comprise patients on other JAK inhibitors, tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) or none (C). The outcome of interest (O) was clinical remission rates, clinical response rates and corticosteroid (CS)-free clinical remission at the assessed time points. Only real-world observational studies with one or two arms were eligible for inclusion (S). We excluded clinical trials, review articles, letters, commentaries, editorials, proceeding research, meeting abstracts, case reports and personal communications. Non-English studies, those involving tofacitinib combined with other biologics as treatment, and studies of patients with mixed Crohn’s disease were also excluded. Eligibility was confirmed by two independent reviewers, and any conflicts or uncertainties were resolved through discussion to reach a consensus. Main outcome measures and data extraction Primary outcomes were clinical remission rate and clinical response rate at various time points. Secondary outcomes were the CS-free clinical remission rate at given time points and adverse effects. Clinical remission was defined as a PMS of less than 3, with a combined stool frequency and rectal bleeding subscale score of 1 or less. Clinical response was defined as a reduction in the PMS by 3 points or more and at least 30% from baseline, along with a decrease of at least 1 point in the rectal bleeding subscale. CS-free clinical remission refers to a state in which a patient achieves and maintains clinical remission without the need for CS therapy. Two independent reviewers read the full text of eligible articles, manually extracted the data and recorded it in Excel. Any inconsistencies were resolved through discussion. The following information was extracted from eligible studies, name of the first author, publication year, study design, country of the study, the number of patients with moderate-to-severe, active UC, mean patient age, the percentage of males, the mean follow-up duration and data regarding the outcomes of interest. Quality assessment The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale (NOS), following the recommendations of the Cochrane Non-Randomised Studies Methods Working Group. 16 The NOS assigns a maximum of 9 points to each study, 4 points for the appropriate selection of patients, 2 points for comparability of participants in terms of design and analysis and 3 points for adequate outcome ascertainment. Two independent reviewers conducted the quality assessment, and any uncertainties were resolved through discussion. Statistical analysis The inverse-variance method, which is based on a weighted average of effect sizes from individual studies, was used to create forest plots displaying proportions with 95% CIs for individual studies and overall studies. Both fixed-effects and random-effects models were applied to calculate the pooled estimates presented in the forest plots. Heterogeneity among the studies was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with the following criteria, 0%–24% indicated no heterogeneity, 25%–49% indicated moderate heterogeneity, 50%–74% indicated large heterogeneity and 75%–100% indicated extreme heterogeneity. Funnel plots were generated, and Egger’s test was applied to detect potential publication bias in the meta-analysis. The meta-analysis was performed using R-studio, and we used the R packages ‘meta,’ ‘dmetar,’ ‘metafor,’ ‘esc’ and ‘tidyverse.’ All analyses were two sided, and a value of p<0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. After the removal of duplicate entries, 168 potentially eligible studies were identified, and a preliminary screening of them was done based on their titles and abstracts. Subsequently, 34 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 15 studies were excluded. Finally, 19 studies 17–35 were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis. Supplementary data bmjgast-11-1-s002.pdf Meta-analysis Clinical response A total of 11 studies 19–22 24 26 27 30 32 33 35 assessed the clinical response rate at various time points. Due to the heterogeneity (I 2 ranging from 64% to 91%) across the studies, estimates by random-effects models were used as the pooled effect. The pooled estimates for clinical response rate were, 0.58 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.67) at week 8, 0.61 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.67) at weeks 12–16, 0.51 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.68) at weeks 24–26 and 0.51 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.77) at week 52 ( figure 2 ). Figure 2 Forest plots for clinical response rate at weeks 8, 12–16, 24–26, and 52. Clinical remission A total of 13 studies 19–24 26 27 29 31–33 35 assessed the clinical remission rate at various time points. Due to the heterogeneity (I 2 ranging from 71% to 78%) across the studies, estimates by random-effects models were used for the pooled effect. The pooled estimates for clinical remission rates were 0.39 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.44) at week 8, 0.43 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.49) at weeks 12–16, 0.40 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.48) at weeks 24–26 and 0.43 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.50) at week 52 ( figure 3 ). Due to the heterogeneity (I 2 ranging from 74% to 88%) across the studies, estimates by random-effects models were used for the pooled effect. The pooled estimates for CS-free clinical remission rates were 0.33 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.41) at week 8, 0.37 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.45) at weeks 12–16, 0.32 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.41) at weeks 24–26 and 0.40 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.50) at week 52 ( figure 4 ). Safety Due to the limited availability of data from only a few studies on serious adverse events (AEs) and infections, a quantitative synthesis could not be conducted. Specifically, Ma et al 23 reported an AE rate of 9.6 serious AEs per 100 person-years, and Deepak et al 17 reported a rate of 10.0 serious AEs per 100 person-years. Straatmijer et al 18 reported a rate of 9.2 serious AEs per 100 person-years, and Shin et al 29 reported a rate of 9.68 per 100 person-years. With respect to infections, Chaparro et al 35 reported an infection rate of 1.67 per 100 person-years, and Ma et al 23 reported a slightly higher rate of 2.1 infections per 100 person-years. Treatment discontinuation rates ranged from 12% to 56.1% among the 15 studies that reported this outcome ( online supplemental table S2 ). Publication bias Funnel plots were created to assess the potential presence of publication bias. Three funnel plots were generated for the outcomes investigated, incorporating data from all study periods. Egger’s regression results suggested no evidence of publication bias, with p values of 0.12 for clinical response rate ( online supplemental figure 1a ), 0.17 for clinical remission rate ( online supplemental figure 1b ) and 0.46 for CS-free clinical remission rate ( online supplemental figure 1c ). Discussion In this updated systematic review and meta-analysis focusing on the real-world use of tofacitinib for treating UC, tofacitinib demonstrated a strong clinical response rate of 61% and a remission rate of 43% during the initial phase of treatment. At 52 weeks, the clinical response rate was 51% and the remission rate was 43%. In addition, the pooled CS-free clinical remission rate in the induction phase was 37%, which increased to 40% at the 1-year follow-up. These results suggest that tofacitinib is an effective option for treating UC, with sustained improvements in UC symptom relief over time. However, the relatively high rates of treatment discontinuation in some studies underscore the need for individualised treatment approaches and ongoing research to optimise the use of tofacitinib for treating UC. Tofacitinib is a small molecule inhibitor of Janus kinases (JAK), which include JAK-1, JAK-2, JAK-3 and TyK-2. 36 37 Tofacitinib primarily inhibits JAK-1 and JAK-3 and is used to treat moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and IBD, including UC. 36 37 The JAKs are important for immune activation and haematopoiesis, and the immunomodulatory effects of tofacitinib are a result of blocking these pathways. 36 37 Risk stratification is important for the use of JAK inhibitors, including tofacitinib, as they may increase the risk of thromboembolic events, and major cardiovascular events in persons 50 years of age and older with pre-existing cardiovascular risk factors. 37 Tofacitinib has become an important treatment for UC worldwide and is especially useful for patients in whom standard conventional or biological treatment have failed or who did not tolerate the treatment. 38 A long list of studies has examined the effectiveness and safety tofacitinib for treating UC and other rheumatic conditions. 38 This has resulted in multiple meta-analyses, mainly based on the results of clinical trials, examining its effectiveness and safety, and overall the studies have shown that tofacitinib is effective in treating UC with a good safety profile. A few systematic reviews or meta-analyses using real-world data have been conducted previously, although with smaller sample sizes and shorter follow-up durations in comparison to the present study. Among, a prior real-world meta-analysis of the effectiveness of tofacitinib for treating UC was published by Taxonera et al . 13 A total of 1162 patients with UC were included, and remission was achieved in 35% of patients at week 8 and 38% at month 6. The response rate was 62% at week 8 and remained high at 51% at 12 months. The incidence of serious AEs and herpes zoster per 100 patient-years was 8.9 and 6.9, respectively. However, that study did not assess 1-year clinical remission rate as evaluated in the present meta-analysis. Moreover, the mentioned meta-analysis incorporated conference abstracts, commonly considered ‘grey literature’, which could hinder the reliability of the pooled results. Another real-world meta-analysis conducted by Lucaciu et al 14 included 830 patients, of which 81% were previously treated with anti-TNF and 57% with VDZ. 14 At week 8, 51% of patients achieved a clinical response and 37% remission. At 24 weeks, the rates were 40% and 29%, respectively. Still, the 1-year remission or response rate documented in the current meta-analysis was not reported by them. Two other recent meta-analyses have found results similar to the two aforementioned studies. Taneja et al 39 examined 26 studies in their meta-analysis and reported clinical response rates of 59% and 51% at week 8 and 1 years, respectively, and remission rates of 30% and 31%, respectively. The pooled incidence of AEs across all dosages was 4.4 per 100 patient-years, and a higher dose was associated with a higher frequency of AEs. CS-free remission rate was not assessed by them. That review also did not exclude meeting abstracts, and results from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and real-world studies were combined together, possibly introducing bias into their findings. Lastly, Macaluso et al 40 performed a meta-analysis of real-world studies that included 759 patients in seven studies. In contrast to our 1-year observation period, that review covered a temporal range of up to 24 to 26 weeks. At induction the clinical response rate was 49%, the clinical remission rate was 40%, and the CS-free clinical remission rate was 34%. Notably, the pooled incidence of AEs was high at 53.0 per 100 person-years, however, this may have been related to the criteria used in the analysis. The OCTAVE Open trial examined the safety and effectiveness of tofacitinib for treating UC, with up to 7 years of treatment. 41 In the analysis of outcomes by 12 months, 9 the efficacy appeared to be better than the outcomes observed in the present meta-analysis of real-world studies. Specifically, after de-escalating tofacitinib, 84.1% sustained a clinical response at 12 months. In the dose escalation group, 64.9% had a clinical response by 12 months, with remission rates of 35.1% and 49.1% at the same intervals, respectively. The difference in observed efficacy between the OCTAVE Open and the present meta-analysis of real-world studies may stem from several factors. First, RCTs are conducted under controlled conditions with strict protocols, often resulting in higher efficacy. Second, RCTs generally involve more homogeneous patient populations, while real-world studies include a broader range of patients with varying stages of disease and comorbidities, which can impact outcomes. Third, patients in real-world settings may not adhere to treatment protocols as closely as those in RCTs, leading to lower observed efficacy. In the final analysis of OCTAVE Open, 41 81.5% of patients initially received tofacitinib 10 mg two times per day. By month 36, clinical response rates were 66.9% for patients on 5 mg and 40.3% for those on 10 mg, with endoscopic improvement seen in 64.6% and 37.1%, and remission maintained or achieved in 58.9% and 33.7%, respectively. With regard to AEs, the incidence rates (2440 patient-years) were death, 0.25, serious infections, 1.61, herpes zoster (all), 3.16 (2.47–3.97), opportunistic infections, 0.87 and major adverse cardiovascular events, 0.16. The incidences of other AEs studied were all ≤1. Discontinuation occurred in 48.0% of patients in the tofacitinib 5 mg bid group and in a much higher proportion, 86.5%, in the tofacitinib 10 mg bid group. Notably, 22.4% of patients in the 10 mg bid group discontinued by month 2 due to insufficient clinical response. The study conclusion was that tofacitinib demonstrated consistent safety up to 7 years. 41 Another recent study examined up to 7.8 years of safety data from the Global Clinical Programme for the treatment of UC with tofacitinib. 42 The incidence rates of AEs were similar to those reported in the aforementioned study, deaths, 0.23, serious infections, 1.69, herpes zoster (all), 3.30 and opportunistic infections, 1.03. Notably, the incidence of major cardiovascular events was 0.29, deep vein thrombosis was 0.03 and pulmonary embolism was 0.19. According to our review, treatment discontinuation ranged from 12% to 56.1% across the studies that reported this outcome. The reasons for tofacitinib discontinuation poststudy enrolment varied. For example, several studies documented that non-response, or a lack of initial therapeutic effect, led to discontinuation as continued treatment was deemed ineffective. 18 19 21–23 31 In other cases, AEs such as serious infections, rash and anaemia necessitated discontinuation due to safety and tolerability concerns. 17–22 24–28 31 33–35 Additionally, loss of response, characterised by initial improvement followed by regression, prompted a strategic reassessment of treatment and subsequent discontinuation. 18 21 26 Another important issue is that, across different outcomes, moderate to large heterogeneity was detected among the studies. This variability likely stems from differences in demographics and treatment histories among the included studies. Such variations challenge the robustness of our interpretations. Additionally, there was significant variability in the patients’ treatment histories, particularly concerning prior exposures to anti-TNF agents, VDZ and UST. These factors might also contribute to the observed heterogeneity. Accordingly, future meta-analyses should consider conducting subgroup analyses to address this heterogeneity when more studies become available. Strengths and limitations The primary strength of this meta-analysis is its comprehensive inclusion and analysis of real-world data, offering insights into the effectiveness of treatment at various time points up to 1 year after beginning treatment. In addition, the meta-analysis included approximately 2600 patients, a more than threefold increase compared with the previous analysis by Lucaciu et al 14 and more than double the number of patients in the review by Taxonera et al . 13 However, notable heterogeneity among the included studies across the outcomes evaluated is a significant limitation of the present meta-analysis. Further, the exclusion of grey literature represents a trade-off. While it can be considered a strength by focusing on peer-reviewed studies only, it may also lead to publication bias, as it potentially omits studies reporting negative or less significant results. Retrospective studies can introduce selection bias, which is a limitation of this meta-analysis. Conclusion This updated meta-analysis supports tofacitinib as an effective treatment for UC in the real world, particularly high clinical response and remission rates during the induction phase and the maintenance period, indicating its potential for long-term symptom relief. Additional meta-analyses to quantitatively synthesise the long-term safety outcomes are highly recommended. Footnotes CW and H-HW contributed equally. documents.title: Acupuncture therapies for postherpetic neuralgia: a protocol for a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common sequela of herpes zoster, and it is often refractory to guideline-recommended treatments. Acupuncture therapy, a wildly applied complementary-alternative treatment, may help in the management of PHN. Diverse types of acupuncture therapy for PHN have been proposed, however, their comparative efficacies remain unclear. This study protocol plans to compare the efficacy and safety of different acupuncture therapies for PHN.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: Databases including MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Chinese Biomedical Database, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP Database, Wanfang Database, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, Chinese Clinical Trial Register and OpenGrey will be searched from their inception to January 2022. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effectiveness of acupuncture therapy on the management of PHN will be selected. The primary outcome is pain intensity. Secondary outcomes include negative emotions, sleep condition, quality of life and adverse events. Reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction and risk of bias assessment procedures. Then, standard pair-wised meta-analysis and Bayesian network meta-analysis will be performed (if applicable). The Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis application will be used to assess the confidence in the evidence for the primary outcome.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: All data used for this study will be extracted from published RCTs, thus, no ethical approval will be required. The results of this systematic review will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journal and conference presentation.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42020219576.
